\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Security agents use language models and tools to solve challenges, exploit
vulnerabilities, and carry out multi-step attack workflows. Benchmarks
evaluate these activities through task outcomes and agent interactions
\cite{cybench,cvebench,incalmo,agentharm}. A recovered key or accepted
exploit is a concrete result. Interpreting it as evidence of autonomous
capability requires knowing how the result was produced, what the
verifier checked, and which attempts contributed to the reported rate.
Claims about speed and reproducibility require further execution records.

Prior work examines benchmark validity, rewards and evaluator
flaws~\cite{abc,agentrewardbench,benchjack,agentsuite}, and establishes
measurement principles for ground truth and experimental
design~\cite{klees,sokfuzzing,benchbench}. We ask which claims retained
security-agent records support and which evidence a stronger inference needs.

Across the recorded studies, the principal results are concrete. A prospective
twelve-session cohort retains eight accepted attack submissions, including
3/3 CBC and 3/3 ECDSA sessions; fixed supplied-operation controls pass 12/12
task oracles; a 45-handshake matrix separates permitted classical fallback from
required hybrid policy; and a controlled side-channel arm attains complete
sixteen-byte key recovery. Historical runs retain key recoveries in 10/23
conditional and 10/51 operational attempts under separately defined
populations. The audit reported here is what makes these outcomes trustworthy:
it corrects verifier identity, recovers undercounted effort, and separates
evaluated capability from metadata and attribution defects.

Our audit finds discrepancies within otherwise accepted executions. In the
R30 escrow session, the submitted key matches the secret's pre-session
commitment, but the result's verifier hash matches an older four-task oracle.
The launcher instead selects the E5-capable verifier. The same session's
terminal request array contains 2,000 entries; retained eviction events
reconstruct 8,714 relay calls. Inspecting deployment reveals a further
distinction: victim containerization and a key-free verifier coexist with
host-executed agent code and unauthenticated escrow delivery. A correct
candidate therefore does not establish the intended secret-access boundary.

The discrepancy recurs in a different form in the prospective agent cohort.
Its twelve sessions retain eight accepted submissions and four rejections,
but none of the eight successful harness durations has a raw monotonic
endpoint pair. Elapsed values remain recorded; their independent
recomputation is unsupported. These are concrete findings about the retained
implementations and executions, not evidence that the accepted candidates
are incorrect or that the agents used an undeclared channel.

The paper contributes both a demonstrated capability baseline and the
empirical audit that makes it trustworthy. We organize the investigation using
\emph{claim-relative evidence assessment}: state a proposition and trust
assumptions, name its required records, then report it as
\emph{supported}, \emph{unresolved}, or \emph{contradicted}.
Execution identity, verifier authority, clock boundaries, counted attempts
and generating components structure the checks. These apply established
measurement and provenance principles to the inspected cases. An executable
replay makes eight bounded decisions inspectable; it is supporting tooling,
rather than an independently validated general auditing method.

Four research questions connect the procedure to its evidence:
\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{1pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item \textbf{RQ1:} Which cryptographic attack tasks are completed by the
retained autonomous-agent cohort?
\item \textbf{RQ2:} How do agent outcomes differ from supplied-operation
reachability and provider-inclusive delivery?
\item \textbf{RQ3:} Where do implementation, interface, and authority
boundaries constrain capability interpretation?
\item \textbf{RQ4:} Which capability statements can be reconstructed from
the retained evidence, and with what unresolved limits?
\end{itemize}

The six-release investigation separates source-level answer flow from
unresolved published-run attribution. Controlled operations, grader cases,
local protocol-policy tests and provenance controls establish positive
properties at their tested boundaries. Timing and historical recovery cases
supply additional measurement contexts (Table~\ref{tab:acts-boundary-map}).
These studies support the central audit; their populations and denominators
remain separate.

The paper makes four contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A provenance-controlled methodology for benchmarking autonomous
cryptographic attack capability.}
A prospective cohort design, fixed supplied-operation controls and
evidence-linked provenance controls make execution attribution an explicit
criterion throughout the procedure
(Sections~\ref{sec:framework}--\ref{sec:results}).
\item \textbf{Separated empirical findings for agent completion,
supplied-executor feasibility, and operational yield.}
Agent completion (8/12 accepted), supplied-executor feasibility (12/12) and
legacy operational yield (10/23 conditional; 10/51 provider-inclusive) are
reported under separately defined populations, without pooling or a causal
model-versus-executor comparison (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
\item \textbf{A capability-boundary characterization retaining both attack
successes and limitations.}
A controlled side-channel arm attains complete sixteen-byte key recovery, and
a 45-handshake matrix separates permitted classical fallback from required
hybrid policy, while answer-flow, verifier-identity, duration and isolation
findings bound what the retained executions establish
(Sections~\ref{sec:results}, \ref{sec:e1} and~\ref{sec:synthesis}).
\item \textbf{An evidence-linked artifact and bounded reproduction package.}
An eight-proposition replay binds decisions to 35 pinned files; operation,
grader, protocol-policy and provenance controls establish their own tested
properties. Required links, trust assumptions and correction witnesses
accompany each decision (Sections~\ref{sec:framework}--\ref{sec:synthesis}).
\end{enumerate}

The supplement maps protocols and historical arms; prior cipher
identification is a separate task~\cite{acts}.

\section{Claim-Relative Evidence Assessment}
\label{sec:framework}

\subsection{Name the claim and its assessment outcome}
Start with a claim about a named task, execution, or population, under
specified conditions. We distinguish five questions.
\emph{Operation validity}: does the candidate satisfy the task's checked
relation? \emph{Agent completion}: did the recorded agent interaction produce
and submit that candidate? \emph{Duration}: what work does the measured
interval cover? \emph{Yield}: which attempts form the success denominator?
\emph{Historical attribution}: do the cited source, configuration, task,
and environment link to the execution that produced the result?
One record can answer some of these questions and leave others open.

For claim $C$ and offered records $R$, identify the required links
$\mathcal{L}(C)$ in Table~\ref{tab:contract}, then inspect each under explicit
trust assumptions. Report \emph{supported} when the applicable links are
established and consistent, \emph{unresolved} when a required link is absent
or ambiguous, and \emph{contradicted} when retained evidence refutes the
proposition. An oracle rejection contradicts correctness of that candidate.
A missing submission trace leaves attribution unresolved. Each outcome
concerns the named claim, rather than the agent's intrinsic ability.

These assessment outcomes are distinct from session-status labels.
\emph{Observed} describes information present in records; \emph{verified}
names a checked candidate relation; \emph{reconstructed} identifies a
quantity derived from retained evidence. \emph{Admissible for a claim} means
that the evidence meets that claim's requirements. Conflicting records
require a stated authority or leave the affected link unresolved.

\paragraph{Executable decisions}
Our supporting checker assigns each required link one of four states:
established, missing, refuted or conflicting. A direct refutation of a
necessary condition contradicts the proposition; otherwise missing or
conflicting evidence leaves it unresolved. Support requires every declared
link. The nonmissing states require a source witness and explanation. The
adapter computes candidate digests, identity joins and event counts from
pinned files; changed bytes stop replay. Authors specify the proposition,
required links and trust assumptions. The checker does not establish the
semantic completeness of those choices or authenticate an arbitrary
recorder. Section~\ref{sec:synthesis} applies this rule to retained cases.

\subsection{Required links and trust assumptions}
Table~\ref{tab:contract} specifies what each answer requires.
Identity connects actions to one execution and prevents duplicate counting.
Verifier authority establishes who owns the checked truth and verdict.
Clock endpoints define the timed work. Census rules define the population.
Provenance binds the execution to its generating components.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Evidence requirements for the named claim. Checks concern retained links; support remains conditional on trusted measurement components.}
\label{tab:contract}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}P{.18\columnwidth}Y P{.28\columnwidth}@{}}
\toprule
\tablehead Boundary & Required evidence/check & Claim enabled \\
\midrule
Execution identity & Task, session and run agree across ordered events, submitted artifact and terminal record; copies identified. & Agent attribution; distinct execution count. \\
Verifier authority & Candidate, checked relation and verdict linked; truth ownership and allowed access established at the claimed boundary. & Operation validity; bounded authority separation. \\
Clock definition & Start/stop events, units, clock source, work included and session binding specified. & Duration of that work; compatible interval comparison. \\
Failure retention & Census, statuses, exclusions and estimator eligibility reconstruct the numerator and denominator. & Yield for the declared population. \\
Provenance & Source, configuration, task and environment identities linked to execution and result. & Historical attribution at the retained stratum. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

The host, operator, harness, oracle, and recording path are trusted measurement
components. A digest identifies bytes; historical use requires a run-linked
record. A process-separation declaration describes an interface property;
isolation against a compromised host requires additional evidence.

The H1 attribution rule requires a direct historical manifest linking exact
source, configuration, task/dataset and immutable environment to execution
and result. The environment component is bounded at the digest-identified
runtime and its declared inputs; host kernel, CPU, external services and any
model provider are trusted components outside that boundary. H2 retains
contemporaneous public components with incomplete
execution linkage. H3 retains static continuity from a dated source candidate
to a later pin. These classes describe different provenance strata.

\paragraph{Worked assessment}
The clean cohort's 12 identities and terminal records retain eight accepted
task relations. Missing raw harness endpoints leave duration reconstruction
unresolved; missing immutable runtime identity gives H1=0/12. Three separate
deterministic controls supply that runtime link and pass H1. These gaps do
not negate the eight checked recoveries.

\subsection{Reconstruct the population before computing yield}
Scheduled identities, physical executions, files, and eligible observations
are different units. Establish a census and duplicate lineage before
selecting an estimator. \emph{Conditional success} uses eligible non-provider
outcomes. \emph{Operational yield} additionally retains provider interruptions
among otherwise eligible observations.

For legacy E2, $54=28$ provider-unavailable $+26$ non-gateway records.
Three relay-invalid cipher block chaining (CBC) records also lack clocks
and are excluded once.
Four further records breach the historical paired-duration gate:
\[
N_{\mathrm{valid}}=26-3=23,\qquad N_{\mathrm{strict}}=23-4=19.
\]
Outcome accounting retains the four valid-graded failures despite their
timing disagreement: conditional success is $10/23=43.5\%$ and eligible
operational yield is $10/(23+28)=10/51=19.6\%$. Only the three relay-invalid
rows are excluded. The frozen timing-selected $10/19$ and $10/47$ remain
historical sensitivities, not the primary outcome estimators. Valid-graded
includes terminal non-successes; strict names the historical selection rule.
The prospective cohort retains all 12 calls with no terminal provider
interruption, so its two denominators coincide. Pilot and escrow records
retain their own populations (Appendix~B.1).

\subsection{Define the interval before interpreting agreement}
$T_M$, also $T_{\mathrm{agent}}$, covers agent execution through terminal
handling, including model latency, construction, tools, and feedback.
$T_{\mathrm{op}}$ covers an already-constructed operation.
$T_{\mathrm{rep}}$ is agent-reported and inherits that reporting trust.
$T_{\mathrm{orc}}$ covers the verifier/escrow graded window.

A time claim identifies start/stop events, units, clock source, recording
party, and included work. Different monotonic windows can include different
interprocess communication, scheduling, and verification work. Legacy analysis imposed a 1~ms
paired-duration gate, naming breaches \texttt{clock\_drift}. That label
records the historical rule, not a demonstrated timer fault. The prospective
contract instead specifies ordered, finite, unit-valid, monotonic,
session-bound endpoints. Section~\ref{sec:architecture} distinguishes this
requirement from implemented checks. V4 retains a source-defined elapsed
difference ending before cleanup and physical session-close logging,
without the raw harness start/stop readings.

\subsection{Analysis families}\label{sec:analysis-labels}
E1 denotes the public-release audit; E2 the legacy agent cohort; E3 the
synthetic timing study; E4 outcome/competing-event analysis; E5 escrow
sessions; and E6 the coding diagnostic. These are family labels, not six
exchangeable experiments. Controls, prospective cohorts and historical arms
retain their own identities and populations in the supplement.

\section{Public Releases: What Is Recoverable?}
\label{sec:e1}

The release audit supports RQ4 by separating two useful forms of evidence:
code that defines an evaluator and records that identify a published
execution. Released source can explain how grading works and enable a new
run. Reconstructing an earlier result additionally requires its interactions
and generating components. We assess both forms at the inspected snapshots.

\subsection{Scope and assessment protocol}
We inspect six purposively selected releases: Cybench and NYU CTF Bench
(CTF solving), CVE-Bench (exploitation), Incalmo (multi-host red teaming),
AgentHarm (misuse), and WebSP-Eval (browser security/privacy). Inspections
and rechecks are dated 27--29 September 2026; a later freeze retains their
source basis. The unit is a release--field pair: six releases and nine
fields produce 54 cells with shared material dependencies.
Selection requires a public paper and inspectable end-to-end artifact across
overlapping task classes, not disjoint strata. Searches follow the named
snapshots' code, output references and archived results; missing links stop
at unresolved evidence. No complete query/candidate-pool log is retained,
so this is a fixed case investigation, not an exhaustive prevalence study.

The audit uses source-linked, AI-assisted worksheets linking judgments
to sources, documentation and recorded artifact searches. Eight graded
worksheet rows plus a reconstruction field form the nine printed fields;
oracle actor and environment are context (Appendix~B.2).
\emph{Yes} means the field's evidence rule is met, \emph{partial} indicates
bounded support, and \emph{no/unverifiable} records insufficient or absent
evidence under that rule. The matrix is frozen. Domain applicability and
source lineage qualify its interpretation. A separate extraction retains
three explicit worksheet domain-N/A notes without regrading the frozen
matrix; other applicability is not independently adjudicated (Appendix~B.2).

The audit asks what the inspected snapshot establishes. Private records
may contain additional evidence. Misuse tasks may have no need to measure
time or label vulnerability primitives, so those statuses alone do not
identify benchmark defects.

\subsection{Released code versus published runs}
\input{tables/tab_audit.tex}
The release profiles distinguish grading behavior, available run records,
and historical linkage. These are separate findings: a missing trajectory
does not refute its published outcome, and a model-based judge is a declared
measurement choice rather than evidence of score manipulation.
The releases expose useful evaluator choices. Incalmo names an
agent-inclusive interval and query/cost accounting; NYU separates model
and tool accounting; CVE-Bench varies zero-day versus one-day starting
information. These positive properties remain part of the field-level
profile. The additional question is whether the released records link
them to the reported executions.

Cybench and NYU CTF Bench implement ordered logging but exclude run-log
directories. CVE-Bench provides challenges and graders without corresponding
published-run records. AgentHarm and WebSP-Eval release task/evaluation
machinery without the authors' evaluation trajectories. Incalmo retains
case-study evidence and an infrastructure-backed replay path, while
full-grid coverage remains unverified.

Archive-level inspection also recovers positive execution evidence:
Incalmo's \texttt{EquifaxLarge} example pairs a result recording 50 infected
hosts and 48 exfiltrated files with 614 action-log entries. This supports
inspection of that example's reported outcome and actions, without
establishing coverage of the published evaluation grid. Cybench's archive
instead retains five output pointers whose Git Large File Storage (LFS)
payloads are unavailable; pointer presence establishes neither their
contents nor the absence of original outputs (Appendix~F.1).

F9 alone implies the all-nine conjunction's 0/6: five no/unverifiable and
one partial. This adds no independent evidence or six failed live
replications. Logger capability is not released-run coverage; Incalmo's
infrastructure requirement is a separate replay constraint.

\subsection{Source-level verifier boundaries}
F2 asks who controls grading truth and verdict state. In-loop grading,
model-mediated judgment, and uncertain state isolation have different
implications. Process co-location alone does not establish answer exposure.
NYU's flag-checking tool holds and prints an answer to console, but that path
alone does not establish model receipt.

At Cybench pin
\texttt{ca483c64\allowbreak 43f17a20\allowbreak ba7d6bac\allowbreak
3d274859\allowbreak a1721e51}, a failed guided subtask inserts its trusted
answer into chat history used by later model calls. A separate local topology
fixture supports parent-memory access under the privileged launcher.
The direct answer-flow finding identifies what information later model calls
can receive in that source version. The fixture separately establishes a
local access property under its launcher.

The answer-flow claim is conditional and directly inspectable: when the
guided-subtask failure branch executes in the inspected implementation,
the trusted answer becomes part of the history supplied to a later model
call. This establishes an evaluation information-flow mechanism. Establishing
its occurrence in a published evaluation would additionally require a
run-linked implementation and configuration, evidence that the guided
branch was enabled and reached, and the resulting model-input history.
Those historical links are unavailable here. Consequently, this finding
cannot quantify affected published tasks or attribute a published success
to answer exposure. Its practical use is to identify the exact branch and
records an evaluator must inspect when distinguishing assisted continuation
from independent subtask completion.

At CVE-Bench pin
\texttt{9fb3e068\allowbreak f260b00d\allowbreak d899ef87\allowbreak
951b88e9\allowbreak c60061f1}, the scorer sits outside the agent loop and
\texttt{/done} supplies bounded feedback. The target nevertheless shares a
security domain with evaluator code/state, leaving isolation after target
compromise unestablished. Retained validation does not demonstrate score
forgery. The two cases distinguish a source-level answer path from an
unresolved grading-domain boundary. Attribution to published runs requires
the additional historical links considered next.

\subsection{Source lineage and historical attribution}
Classify components before assigning a cell's provenance: its material
dependencies bound the available attribution. H1 requires the run-linked
manifest defined in Section~\ref{sec:framework}. Timestamp proximity and
matching source bytes alone leave execution identity unresolved.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Source basis for the 54 E1 cells. Provenance and semantic evidence status are separate assessments.}
\label{tab:provenance-summary}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}lrY@{}}
\toprule
\tablehead Class & Cells & Retained source basis \\
\midrule
H1 & 0 & Complete historical source/configuration/dataset/environment link. \\
H2 & 14 & Contemporaneous public component; execution linkage absent. \\
H3 & 7 & Static continuity from a dated source candidate to a later pin. \\
L1 & 24 & Later pinned implementation; historical linkage not established. \\
S1 & 6 & Published artifact/result; generating implementation unlinked. \\
U1 & 3 & Material identity or hash dependency unresolved. \\
\midrule
Total & 54 & Each field cell has one provenance class. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

The H1 total is 0/54. H2=14 and H3=7 retain contemporaneous-component
and static-continuity evidence; L1=24, S1=6 and U1=3 identify later-source,
published-result and unresolved bases. These are dependent descriptions
of six assessments, not 54 replications. Static comparison preserves
claim-critical Cybench paths from an earlier candidate to the later pin
without fixing the runtime. CVE-Bench's later pin and closer paper-time
candidate differ materially in grader code (Appendix~B.3).

\subsection{Assessment uncertainty}
The original AI re-derivation reports 46/54 agreement,
$\kappa=0.78$, eight adjacent disagreements and zero full reversals.
Its vocabulary includes reconstruction labels preceding the printed
matrix's normalization. It is a diagnostic on the same frozen material;
it is not independent inter-assessor validation of the printed judgments.

Disagreements locate thresholds such as model-label pinning versus generated
artifact identity, and hints versus discovery/execution separation.
Appendix~B.6 retains a separate output lineage and its limitations.
No independent alternative-rubric sensitivity study is available.
Consequently, the reproducible audit object is the field rule, inspected
material and evidence pointer, with assessor uncertainty explicit.

\paragraph{Context for RQ4}
The audit yields a claim-specific profile of evaluator design, answer flow,
and historical linkage. Its useful output is the source or run record
supporting each judgment and the particular record still missing.
The execution studies next test those links directly, using the same
requirements for our own outcomes.

\section{Executed Evidence and Security Cases}
\label{sec:results}

The retained executions demonstrate concrete, checkable attack outcomes.
Under the frozen prospective contract, agent sessions constructed and
submitted accepted attack candidates in 8 of 12 scheduled cells, including
3/3 CBC and 3/3 ECDSA sessions; the fixed executor passes 12/12 supplied
operations (Section~\ref{sec:architecture}); the legacy loop retains ten
successes among 23 eligible challenge records (10/23, 43.5\% conditional) and
ten of 51 under provider-interruption accounting (10/51, 19.6\% operational
yield). Server group policy changes the same client condition from
5/5 completion to 5/5 rejection across 45 checked handshakes, and the escrow
arm verifies one submitted candidate directly against a pre-session
commitment. The remainder of this section substantiates each result, states
the links each one retains, and reports the cases where a stronger claim is
not yet supported. Section~\ref{sec:analysis-labels} decodes the analysis
families; their populations remain separate.

\subsection{Agent outcomes require a defined population}
The legacy loop plans, writes, executes and submits code for RC4 keystream
reuse, ChaCha20 nonce reuse, CBC padding-oracle recovery and ECDSA nonce
reuse. The retained census has 54 rows: 28 provider-unavailable and 26
non-gateway. Excluding the three relay-invalid CBC rows leaves 23 valid
outcomes and ten successes. Four further failures breach the historical
clock gate; they remain in outcome rates. The 19-row strict subset is
retained only as a timing-selected historical sensitivity.

The four clock exclusions are gpt-4o-mini's three ECDSA repetitions and
RC4 repetition 2; they remain valid-graded failures. The 26 September 2026
UTC campaign has six mutable OpenRouter labels and unequal paid/free coverage
(Appendix~C.2). These conditions and the very small CBC/ECDSA populations
bound any comparison.

Surviving transcripts expose parser errors, malformed/double-escaped code,
execution errors and no-claim endings. The CBC note records missing imports
and incorrect block modification before relay failure. An early ECDSA
prompt omitted a verifier-required field; early filenames overwrote some
transcripts. These records identify failure mechanisms without estimating
their frequency. The accepted RC4/ChaCha20 candidates demonstrate achieved
recoveries for the configured loop. Zero legacy CBC/ECDSA successes leave
intrinsic ability unresolved.

\subsection{A complete census retains eight accepted agent results}
The prospective arm freezes four tasks and three repetitions ($N=12$),
the prequalified APMIX access path and exact label
\texttt{claude-sonnet-4-6-free}, settings, budgets, scheduled-cell policy
and task/prompt/source/oracle/writer/schema identities before its calls.
Each cell runs once without replacement. The loop separately permits
transient-request retries, whose individual attempt count is not retained.

Task-specific verdict review finds explicit acceptance in eight and explicit
rejection in four; fallback classification is unnecessary to explain

observations. Appendix~C.5 preserves the final namespace and hashes.

\subsection{Provenance controls establish an attainable attribution criterion}
The clean records establish identity, submission, and terminal coverage.
This is sufficient to inspect the eight accepted task relations and four
rejections. Output tails bound byte retention, and raw harness start/stop
readings are absent for all eight successful durations. Logged elapsed values
remain descriptive; independent duration reconstruction is unresolved.
Validator acceptance also leaves some endpoint and isolation requirements
untested. Each gap affects its corresponding claim under the declared contract.

EXP-034 retains source, task, execution, artifact and result links, but lacks
immutable runtime identity: H1=0/12. It is the representative missing-component
negative control.
\label{sec:exp035}
EXP-035 binds source, configuration, task, oracle, a content-addressed
Open Container Initiative (OCI) environment, run, artifact, result and clocks in three deterministic
read-only executions. All pass the unchanged H1 rule (3/3), without a
provider/model call. The environment link pins the digest-identified local
runtime and its read-only, network-disabled inputs; host kernel, CPU, external
services and any provider remain trusted components outside that boundary.
This implementation demonstration shows that the rule can be satisfied by
retaining the required execution links; it claims neither necessity, sufficiency
nor reliability for a networked agent with mutable backend state. The two
populations test different links and leave E1 unchanged.

\subsection{Protocol, recovery, and wire-editing cases test different claims}
\label{sec:historical-boundary-probes}
\paragraph{Server policy controls local protocol completion}
C2b asks whether allowing classical fallback and requiring a hybrid group
produce different outcomes for the same client condition. Endpoint
transcripts agree on the parsed negotiated key-share group, and pooled
verdicts match the predeclared table, for all 45 loopback handshakes
across nine cells. Holding client bytes, build, and host fixed, changing
server group policy changes the classical-only condition from 5/5 completion
to 5/5 rejection. Hybrid-capable and incompatible-group controls validate
the local verdict machinery (Appendix~D.1). The intervention therefore
identifies server policy as the enforcement point for these endpoints.

Acceptance is determined from parsed wire evidence: the ServerHello key-share
group and Finished messages, checked against both endpoint traces.
Rejection requires the recorded handshake-failure alert and absence of
Finished. The hybrid-capable positive control establishes that the required
configuration can complete; the incompatible-group control establishes that
the same machinery detects rejection. Thus the allow/require difference
cannot be explained solely by an always-accepting verdict or a server that
fails every connection. A client application-data record is retained
separately; in TLS 1.3 its outer record type alone does not evidence
decrypted payload; acceptance rests on the Finished messages instead.
The implemented channel check is not a bidirectional echo test.

A separate exploratory order check offers X25519 before X25519MLKEM768
to the allowing server. In this build the client's initial key share follows
its configured first group: the offer lists X25519 first with an

cell against the same server lists X25519MLKEM768 first with a hybrid key
share and negotiates the hybrid group in 5/5. Order and key share change together, so the arm isolates

Outcome reanalysis gives 10/23 conditional success (43.5\%) and 10/51
eligible operational yield (19.6\%), retaining all four clock-disagreement

The pilot's 20 retained sessions include 17 provider interruptions, one
success, one timeout and one tool failure (Appendix~C.3).
These endings describe the observed process; continuation under restored
access is a separate assumption-dependent question.

\subsection{E3: a synthetic workload contrast measured across process spans}
E3 compares two synthetic C programs, each running 20,000 iterations.
The V build uses an indexed table lookup; CT scans all 256 entries to
select the same value. Both compile with \texttt{-O2} and
\texttt{-fno-strict-aliasing}. The deliberately different work supplies
a build contrast, not an AES leakage or key-recovery experiment.

Every trial starts a fresh subprocess. Both capture arms measure its wall

records child user CPU time. Before cold trials the driver runs
\texttt{sync} and writes 3 to Linux \texttt{drop\_caches}, outside the timed

The 32,000 records comprise two builds, two arms, two cache-operation labels
and two simultaneous multithreading (SMT) labels, 2,000 trials per cell.
The retained initial driver applies SMT while preparing both blocks, before
the trial loop; the resume code applies it per remaining block. The
15,971-record interrupted prefix has no per-trial hardware-state attestation.

The verified-order resume adds no independent repetition. These one-host
process spans cannot substitute for an agent-completion interval.

arm/cache/SMT setting gives eight differences. Their median is

with control random-seed samples. Its PASS therefore establishes neither
within-vulnerable leakage sensitivity nor constant-time assurance.

Intervals remain conditional on the host, recorded blocks and resampling
design. They characterize process spans, not CPU-cache leakage or an
independently validated agent-completion clock. Appendix~C.6 retains all cells,

\subsection{Escrow links a recovery to a pre-session commitment}
Recomputing SHA-256 from R30's submitted 128-bit candidate reproduces the
pre-session commitment and escrow verification digest. The escrow log has
one generation, one delivery, one successful comparison, and no reveal.
Candidate correctness is therefore checked directly from retained bytes,
under the stated host/operator trust.

E5 asks whether a submitted recovery matches a secret committed before the
session under the recorded authority path. Escrow generates and commits a
fresh secret, provisions the victim, receives candidate comparisons, and logs
verification/reveal order. The verifier forwards candidates without owning
the secret. Reveal follows a verification attempt, including a rejection.
These fractions count checked candidates, not autonomous recovery under
enforced secret isolation. The initial four sessions yield 0/4; the extension
yields 1/10. Their descriptive total is 1/14, separate from E2; unavailable
launches remain visible outside this graded fraction (Appendix~C.7).
The retained session contains three model turns and three generated-code
executions. Its final code ranks key-byte candidates using chosen plaintexts
and the victim's explicit \texttt{/footprint} page sets. This is a
purpose-built leakage interface, not a measured cache-timing attack.
The request array retains only its last 2,000 entries. Together with 6,714
\texttt{http\_request\_log} eviction events and the source's one-entry
eviction rule, it reconstructs 8,714 relayed HTTP calls. The retained tail
alone understates effort. Its graded span is 222.6975~s. These records let a
reader inspect the candidate relation and authority path together. The
matching candidate and submitted code support
the recorded recovery through this interface, while the launch/access
defects in Section~\ref{sec:architecture} prevent a claim of enforced
blinding. The span covers the graded window; reconstructed relay calls do
not count arbitrary host-side activity or provider requests.
The record's oracle hash identifies the older four-task oracle: the builder
hashes that file although the launcher selects the E5-capable verifier.
This is a verifier-identity defect, distinct from the independently checked
candidate/commitment relation (Appendix~C.7).

Verdicts and submissions answer RQ2; intervals, populations, and provenance
answer RQ3. Halted campaigns, the 180-case synthetic fault control, and
local-model launch failures retain instrumentation roles (Appendix~D.2).

\section{Empirical Corrections and Their Reproduction}
\label{sec:synthesis}

This section reports two results: verified attack outcomes on retained
executions, and the corrections that the same records provoke. The replay
in Table~\ref{tab:synthesis} checks eight
propositions over 35 pinned source and observation files. Four are
supported, three contradicted and one unresolved. These are related
propositions on retained cases, not eight independent experiments or an
assessment-accuracy estimate.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Eight replayed propositions. The same retained execution can support candidate correctness and contradict a metadata or effort claim. Trust and source witnesses accompany the machine-readable outputs.}
\label{tab:synthesis}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}P{.27\columnwidth}P{.20\columnwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
\tablehead Proposition & Assessment & Decisive evidence \\
\midrule
Clean cohort retains eight accepted submissions & Supported & Twelve unique identities; transcript and record verdicts agree; accepted runs link code and claims. \\
All 12 clean sessions succeed & Contradicted & Four terminal sessions lack acceptance. \\
Eight successful harness durations can be recomputed & Unresolved & Eight elapsed values, zero raw harness endpoint pairs. \\
R30 candidate matches a pre-session commitment & Supported & Candidate bytes, escrow digest and commitment agree; event order checked. \\
R30 retained escrow log contains no reveal & Supported & No reveal event in the inspected log; no access-isolation inference. \\
R30 verifier digest identifies retained V2 source & Contradicted & Recorded digest matches the older oracle, not the V2 source selected by the launcher. \\
R30's 2,000-entry array is total relay effort & Contradicted & 6,714 one-entry eviction events precede the retained tail. \\
R30 records reconstruct 8,714 relay calls & Supported & Tail plus eviction count under the inspected recorder rule. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\subsection{From a result label to an evidential decision}
The clean cohort supports eight candidate relations while leaving duration
reconstruction unresolved. Missing endpoints neither negate the checked
recoveries nor become sufficient timing evidence merely because a candidate
was accepted.

The complementary security cases retain their tested scope in
Table~\ref{tab:acts-boundary-map}. The 20 deterministic grader cases test
interface behavior; R30 instead supplies an observed candidate/commitment
relation under the deployed escrow path. Host/operator trust remains explicit.

Tracing the recorder itself changes a further conclusion: R30's 2,000-entry
HTTP array is a bounded tail, while its eviction events reconstruct 8,714
relay calls. Tracing deployment distinguishes a key-free verifier from an
agent-inaccessible secret, because generated code executes on the host and
escrow requests lack caller authentication. These are concrete corrections
produced by following a claim through records and implementation, rather
than treating an accepted schema or a role diagram as sufficient evidence.

\subsection{Replaying corrections rather than a benchmark score}
The replay independently reads the retained records, transcripts and source
digests instead of accepting the paper's summary values. It joins the clean
INDEX to twelve distinct records, checks terminal verdict agreement and
accepted submission paths, hashes the R30 candidate without exporting its
secret bytes, checks commitment order, and counts request evictions.
The verifier comparison concerns retained source bytes; it does not recover
an unrecorded historical runtime. The effort computation assumes the pinned
recorder's one-entry eviction rule and complete retained truncation events.
Eleven software tests exercise missing and conflicting links, direct
refutation, source drift and preservation of correctness despite an
unrelated metadata defect. Matching author-derived expectations validates
these software behaviors, not independent semantic accuracy.

We also apply selected ABC guidance to the same cases~\cite{abc}.
Its environment and interpretation checks motivate qualifying clean runtime
and duration claims. Its ground-truth separation check motivates inspecting
the R30 launch path. The resulting concerns are compatible with our
findings; the replay adds explicit proposition-level outputs and the
2,000-to-8,714 effort reconstruction. This is an analytic comparison, not
evidence of better detection than ABC, BenchJack or COBA. The empirical
contribution lies in the demonstrated recoveries together with the
inspected mechanisms, corrected quantities and their source witnesses. Appendix~F.3 supplies case requirements and replay
paths; independent assessor reliability remains unmeasured.

Appendix~E.1 separately reconstructs historical SP2-05 sessions and migration
duplicates; neither copies nor summaries add executions to this audit.

\paragraph{Answers to RQ1--RQ4}
Task completion (RQ1): retained agent sessions yield oracle-accepted
submissions in 8/12 scheduled cells of the prospective cohort (RC4 0/3,
ChaCha20 2/3, CBC 3/3, ECDSA 3/3); the RC4 zero is a cohort outcome rather
than evidence of inability.
Execution-mode and operational distinctions (RQ2): supplied operations succeed
12/12 and remain separate from agent sessions, whose legacy records give 10/23
conditional success (43.5\%) and 10/51 provider-inclusive operational yield
(19.6\%).
Capability boundaries (RQ3): each demonstrated capability is bounded by its
tested interface and authority; local group policy, host-qualified timing,
modified-victim recovery and an accepted escrow candidate are not primitive
breaks, stock recovery or enforced blinding.
Reconstructable evidence (RQ4): the replay reconstructs four of the eight
checked propositions, corrects three, and leaves successful-duration
recomputation (0/8) unresolved; EXP-035's 3/3 passes in a no-model control
show bounded provenance attainability.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Agent capability and execution}
Cybench and NYU CTF Bench evaluate CTF solving; CVE-Bench and Incalmo examine
exploitation and multi-host workflows; AgentHarm and WebSP-Eval cover misuse
and browser security/privacy tasks
\cite{cybench,nyuctf,cvebench,incalmo,agentharm,webspeval}.
AgentBench and ASB broaden interactive settings~\cite{agentbench,asb}.
These workloads motivate the release audit. Our four cryptographic tasks
provide controlled candidate relations for testing execution and verification
evidence, with task scope stated separately from agent generality.

AgentDojo studies prompt-injection attacks/defenses~\cite{agentdojo}.
IsolateGPT and SAGA address execution isolation and agent security
architecture~\cite{isolategpt,saga}. AgentBoard supplies analytical progress
views, MATE audits trajectories against policies, and agentic-AI
systematization examines tool-execution boundaries
\cite{agentboard,mate,sokagent}. Their mechanisms and analyses concern what
agents do and may access. Our assessment asks which inference their retained
execution evidence supports.

\paragraph{Validity and evaluator audits}
ABC gives task/outcome validity and reporting guidelines~\cite{abc}.
BenchJack adversarially discovers reward-hacking paths and iteratively
repairs benchmarks~\cite{benchjack}. AgentSuite/COBA examines user,
environment, ground-truth and evaluation components through rule and
model-based filtering~\cite{agentsuite}. These close precedents establish
why evaluation components require scrutiny. ABC already addresses
ground-truth isolation, frozen environments and result interpretation;
these principles are foundations of our investigation, rather than claimed
inventions. Our empirical addition follows retained security executions
through candidate checks, recorder code and metadata: a verified commitment
match coexists with an incorrect verifier digest and an effort count that
must be reconstructed from eviction events. Section~\ref{sec:synthesis}
applies relevant ABC guidance to those same records. We report an analytic
comparison and reproducible corrections, not comparative auditor accuracy
or independently validated general-purpose method effectiveness.

AgentRewardBench compares automatic trajectory judgments with expert
assessments~\cite{agentrewardbench}. Our AI diagnostic lacks that independent
authority. Our procedure retains the evidential basis of
each proposition: judgment accuracy, session coverage, and historical
attribution can differ even for one accepted candidate.
Table~\ref{tab:early-novelty} summarizes the respective assessment objects.
\input{NOVELTY_COMPARISON_TABLE}

\paragraph{Measurement and provenance}
Fuzzing-evaluation research motivates controlled targets, ground truth,
repetitions and defensible analysis~\cite{klees,sokfuzzing}.
Agent-evaluation research adds cost and reproducibility~\cite{kapoor};
PROV-AGENT records prompts, outputs, decisions and workflow
context~\cite{provagent}. We apply those principles to mutable access paths
and historical security claims. Prior ACTS classification results concern
cipher identification~\cite{acts}. Cache-timing/constant-time research
contextualizes E3's narrower synthetic process-span study~\cite{bernstein,osvik,dudect}; Kaplan--Meier supplies the
secondary continuation analysis with its censoring assumptions~\cite{kaplanmeier}.
Together, these precedents motivate both the recording mechanisms and
the inference checks used in our execution studies.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Tracing security-agent results through their generating records reveals
specific discrepancies that an accepted outcome alone does not expose.
R30's candidate matches a pre-session commitment, while its verifier digest
identifies an older oracle and its bounded request array understates relay
effort: retained evictions reconstruct 8,714 calls. Deployment inspection
also distinguishes key-free grading from enforced secret isolation.
The clean cohort retains eight accepted submissions in twelve sessions,
but none of the eight successful harness durations has raw endpoint pairs.

The paper's results are twofold. First, agent-executed cryptographic
attacks are demonstrated under recorded conditions: eight accepted
submissions in twelve prospective sessions, including 3/3 CBC and 3/3 ECDSA
task coverage; a fixed-executor baseline of 12/12; a 45-handshake
protocol-policy matrix; a sixteen-byte side-channel recovery under the
Spread-Table record; and a candidate verified against a pre-session
commitment. Second, the release audit separates source-level mechanisms
from their unresolved occurrence in published executions and supplies an
executable eight-proposition replay over 35 pinned files with source
witnesses for the central retained cases. Operation, protocol-policy,
grader and provenance controls retain their narrower positive results; the
assessment structure applies established measurement principles without
claiming independent general-method validation. Correct outcomes and
corrected interpretations remain visible together.

\section{Recording Executions and Checking Claims}
\label{sec:architecture}

The harness is the controller that reserves executions, records agent
interactions, and retains outcomes; task-specific checkers, called oracles,
verify submitted candidates, so every reported recovery is bound to a
recorded execution and a checked relation. Together they make the
demonstrated outcomes and their evidence requirements inspectable. We distinguish the declared \emph{contract}, checks implemented
in code, and properties exercised by \emph{controls}; each has its own
evidential basis.

\subsection{Actors, authority, and trust assumptions}
Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} separates agent, target, verifier, escrow and
recording roles. The agent controls generated code and candidates. The target
exposes a purpose-built vulnerable interface. The verifier owns the checked
relation and verdict; the harness owns identity, recording and terminal
classification. Analyst eligibility subsequently selects a population.

Reserved configuration provisions the target; the model receives public
inputs and permitted queries. Victim secrets are part of the task, whereas
grader memory and logs are outside the declared interface. Host and operator
trust remain. The controls address malformed candidates, metadata
substitution, replay, cross-session reuse, missing outcomes and clock
conflation at specified interfaces.
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_architecture}
\caption{Capture-first architecture and verification authority. Solid arrows show the task and capture paths. The dashed arrow marks E5 escrow provisioning; the verifier forwards the candidate for escrow comparison and retains the resulting verdict. Ordinary task oracles retain their own task ground truth, while the E5 verifier does not own the secret. The record binds events, artifacts, clocks, and terminal status for subsequent eligibility analysis. The diagram specifies roles and interfaces, not a proof of host-level isolation.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Preparation, capture, and closure}
\paragraph{Preparation}
Before provider invocation, the driver checks existing records/transcripts
and atomically reserves the run identity. A collision is rejected; a crash
leaves a reservation for inspection. Task-card digests and source,
configuration and access metadata bind intended conditions. Provider routing
labels identify an access path with mutable backend state.

\paragraph{Capture}
Ordered model turns, tool calls, generated artifacts, candidate submissions
and oracle events link actions to outcomes. Session, operation and oracle
timing fields name separate windows. Tool stdout/stderr uses bounded tails;
a parse-error branch retains a response prefix. Thus the retained objects
support event reconstruction with bounded byte coverage.

\paragraph{Closure}
The builder binds task, model/access configuration, environment, artifacts
and summary. The writer validates records and uses exclusive creation to
refuse overwrite. Partial records require reconciliation with reservations;
publication is not atomic across all files.

The inherited validator checks status/success consistency, duration fields
and their difference, and oracle/hash metadata. V4 relaxes duration-agreement
tolerance. Its acceptance does not check every required endpoint, ordering,
unit or session-binding property. Likewise, \texttt{separate\_process}
declares separation without testing isolation. The clean cohort therefore
tests identity and terminal retention while duration reconstruction and
immutable runtime attribution remain unresolved (Appendix~C.5).

\subsection{Task and escrow verdicts}
The ordinary oracle retains fresh ground truth in its own process.
RC4 and ChaCha20 acceptance checks recovered plaintext. The CBC
padding-oracle task checks the declared padded/unpadded
plaintext relation. The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
task checks both a reserved private key and a valid challenge signature.
Each accepted verdict therefore states exactly which recovery relation
was verified.

The fixed-operation control exercises distinct recovery mechanisms. RC4 and
ChaCha20 reuse a keystream: supplied ciphertext relations permit plaintext
recovery, which the oracle compares with its reserved plaintext. CBC permits
adaptive padding-validity queries and checks the recovered plaintext after
padding normalization. ECDSA supplies two signatures sharing a nonce and a
new challenge message; acceptance requires both the reserved private scalar
and a valid challenge signature. A valid signature under an unrelated claimed
key is insufficient. These relations explain what the 12 accepted operations
establish before an agent's construction process is considered.

E5 places secret generation and comparison in escrow. A commitment precedes
the session; the victim receives the secret and the verifier forwards
candidates. The retained controller compares in constant time and logs
generation, delivery, verification and reveal. Reveal requires a preceding
attempt, including unsuccessful attempts. Agent attribution additionally
requires the interaction and submission path; trusted host/operator channels
remain outside the controls' demonstrated isolation boundary.

\paragraph{Environment and verification boundaries}
Table~\ref{tab:e5-access} distinguishes deployed authority from intended
roles. Key-free comparison establishes a candidate relation, not its
acquisition path.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Actual E5 authority. Host trust does not imply agent-to-secret isolation.}
\label{tab:e5-access}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}lY@{}}
\toprule
\tablehead Actor & Retained location and authority \\
\midrule
Agent code & Host subprocess; dedicated agent sandbox not established. \\
Victim & Key-bearing container; service published on host loopback. \\
Verifier & Host process forwards candidates; grading state owns no key. \\
Escrow & Host listener owns key; delivery/reveal lack caller authentication. \\
Controller & Trusted host provisioning/logging; role names are not access enforcement. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

R30 retains victim image digest/lifecycle and host Python, OS, OpenSSL,
compiler and Docker strings, not an immutable whole environment.
Escrow binds to \texttt{0.0.0.0}; reveal checks attempt order, not caller
authority. Victim containment and key-free grading have source/event support;
agent-to-secret isolation lacks enforcement in this launch path. The separate
protected fixture tests only its own interface behavior.

\subsection{Terminal classification and eligibility}
The classifier prioritizes available oracle outcomes, then recognized
provider/harness errors, then behavioral endings. A fired budget precedes a
later give-up. Remaining branches distinguish refusal, give-up and tool
failure. The fallback is \texttt{ORACLE\_FAIL}; only the underlying verdict
and interaction show whether a candidate was submitted and rejected.

Eligibility follows the claim. A candidate can remain a verified recovery
while missing endpoints exclude independent duration reconstruction.
Identity defects affect counting separately: the halted 270-session design
stopped at 33 scheduled graded sessions; 38 source rows represented 32
physical records with 10 identity defects. Its gate withheld capability
rates, timing summaries and rankings (Appendix~D.2).

\subsection{Controls and demonstrated properties}
All 20 deterministic protected-grader cases match their expected outcomes.
This is the separate in-process \texttt{E5-CONTROLLED} fixture, not the
network handler used by the E5 agent sessions. Its parser and session binder
exercise valid, malformed, substituted, stale, and replayed requests.
Grading-state read/write probes call explicit denial methods; they do not
attempt arbitrary process-memory or filesystem access. The two valid cases
are accepted; the remaining 18 cases are rejected or denied. The synthetic
vulnerable comparator exposes and changes its own state by construction.
These tests establish the specified API behavior, not deployment isolation.

The fixed executor performs four operations with three fresh-secret
repetitions each, without a model loop or retries: 12/12 pass task oracles.
The prospective agent arm freezes its four tasks, three repetitions,
provider/model path, prompts/cards, source/oracle/writer/schema hashes,
budgets and eligibility before invocation. Scheduled cells run once without
replacement. The loop permits up to three transient transport attempts
within a turn; their individual retry census is absent.

Together these controls fix the positive baseline of the paper: the fixed
operations are reachable and reproducible (12/12), the protected-grader
interface enforces its declared acceptance and denial behavior (all 20
cases), and prospective sessions retain identity, interactions, and terminal
coverage. The evidence assessment records the remaining implementation gaps
alongside these positive results.

\subsection{Qualification and rejection controls}
Separate deterministic controls test whether the task interface accepts fresh
instances and rejects stale or malformed inputs before interpreting agent
outcomes. Contract V3-04 accepts all four configured operations (4/4);
the CBC operation makes 10,775 oracle queries. The regression record retains
eight successful freshness cases and rejects missing arguments, malformed
JSON, stale hard-coded outputs, duplicate run identities, cross-session
identity substitution, and stale artifacts. Terminal-status mappings also
match the declared cases. Two additional qualification branches each retain
2/2 successes (Appendix~F.2).

These controls make interface reachability, freshness, rejection behavior,
and identity enforcement inspectable. Their units are deterministic test
cases, distinct from agent sessions and the protected-grader fixture.

\section{Scope, Responsibility, and Artifacts}
\label{sec:limitations}

\subsection{Scope of inference}
E1 assesses six purposively selected snapshots. They are not independent
cells or fresh published-run replications. Domain-sensitive judgments, the F9-driven
conjunction and provenance definitions bound its findings.

The twelve clean sessions use one mutable backend, three per task; they
support neither model rankings nor clean/legacy causal comparisons.
Uneven legacy coverage, prompt/harness defects, missing transcripts and
historical-record limits further constrain attribution.

E3 measures synthetic process spans under filesystem-cache operations.
SMT rows stratify recorded labels; the interrupted prefix lacks per-trial
state attestation. The resume supplies no independent block/host
replication. E5's small unmatched populations leave causal escrow effects
unidentified. The three deterministic provenance controls test H1
attainability under host/operator trust and contain no agent/provider.

\subsection{Procedure and implementation limits}
The five boundaries cover the examined claims; their completeness across
other evaluation settings is untested. The researcher audit and shared-packet
AI diagnostic provide no independent inter-assessor reliability estimate.
Reproduction of a worksheet or schema check does not independently validate
its semantic judgment.

Implementation gaps have specific consequences. Missing raw harness
endpoints for all eight successful clean durations prevent independent
duration reconstruction. Untested structural clock checks and process
isolation constrain timing and authority guarantees. Bounded output tails
and response-prefix capture constrain byte coverage, while uncounted
transient-request retries leave request-level effort unresolved.
Task verdicts and the session census remain inspectable; stronger claims
require the corresponding additional capture or validation evidence.

\subsection{Safety and research responsibility}
Execution studies use local purpose-built vulnerable services and generated
secrets under project control. Source forensics and fixtures retain different
evidence from exploitation of published runs. Provider interruptions,
refusals, harness faults and rejected candidates retain their own attribution.
Researcher/AI assessments, agent actions and deterministic verdicts are
identified by their respective sources.

The source audit examines released implementations and retained snapshots;
its local fixtures do not test deployed third-party systems. Task verdicts,
candidate relations, and source findings are checked through the evidence
paths described in Sections~\ref{sec:architecture}--\ref{sec:results}.
The authors determine that the source-audit findings are disclosable
research-artifact defects rather than deployed-system exploits, and will
send evidence-bounded notifications to the affected benchmark maintainers
before submission; no notification has been sent as of this revision. The
author-side corpus contains candidate secrets and identifying paths, so
public release requires redaction and anonymity review. Prior
cipher-identification work is cited in the third person~\cite{acts}.

\subsection{Artifact and reproduction boundary}
The artifact maps claims to task cards, source/configuration/oracle hashes,
observations, transcripts, analyses, and population rules (Appendix~F.1).
All 50 existing discovery-ledger entries have a documented placement or
disposition across the paper, supplement, and artifact. This makes the
known strengths, intentional exclusions, historical aliases, and unavailable
payloads discoverable. The ledger also preserves non-Git evidence and
incomplete campaigns. Its named discovery gaps remain open; this crosswalk
establishes coverage of the indexed entries.

Reanalysis of retained bytes and repetition through a mutable provider are
different reproduction operations. Current code cannot restore missing
historical runtime identity. Numerical locks check arithmetic and declared
consistency; source inspection and retained events determine the semantic
claim. Independent replication and isolation beyond the tested interfaces
remain separate validation questions.
